title: Practical Meat Inspection of Small Stock

lessons.title: Ante-mortem inspection of sheep and goats
lessons.html:
Small stock in the lairage

Sheep and goats come to the abattoir in large groups, often from many farms in one truck. Inspect them in the lairage before slaughter as required by the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Watch the flock at rest, then make them move so you can see lame or weak animals.

What to look for

  • Fleece and skin: heavy dirt or dung (daggy wool), scab or mange, wounds, blowfly strike, lumps and swellings.
  • Lumps under the skin: swollen lymph nodes in front of the shoulder or in the flank can point to caseous lymphadenitis.
  • Head: nasal discharge, sneezing, swollen jaw, sores on lips (orf).
  • Breathing and condition: coughing, laboured breathing, very thin animals, swollen bellies.
  • Movement: lameness, foot rot, animals lagging behind the group.
  • Identification: ear tags or tattoos and the movement documents.

Decisions

Pass normal animals for slaughter. Separate suspect animals in a sick pen for the veterinarian. Very dirty or wet sheep may need to be held until they dry, or slaughtered at the end of the day with extra care, because dirty fleece contaminates the carcass during skinning. Report suspected notifiable diseases immediately and keep the group apart.

Humane handling

Never lift sheep by the wool, legs or tail and never throw them off a truck. Lifting by the wool causes bruises that must later be trimmed. Move sheep calmly with boards or flags, using their natural flocking. Goats should not be pulled by the horns or ears. Rough handling is an offence under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 and lowers carcass quality.

lessons.title: Head and offal inspection in small stock
lessons.html:
Head

Look at the head for abscesses, wounds and swelling of the jaw. Larvae of the sheep nasal bot fly may be found in the nasal passages. Follow your abattoir's procedure for which head parts are inspected, used or condemned.

Red offal

Lungs

View and palpate. Look for pneumonia, lungworm nodules, abscesses and hydatid cysts, which are fluid-filled bladders caused by the dog tapeworm Echinococcus. Incise the bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes when required.

Heart

View and incise the heart muscle to look for sheep measles (Cysticercus ovis), small white cysts in muscle caused by a dog tapeworm. Look for inflammation of the heart sac.

Liver

View and palpate. Look for:

  • Liver fluke: thickened bile ducts, flukes in the ducts.
  • Bladder worms (Cysticercus tenuicollis): thin-walled cysts hanging on the liver or the fatty omentum, also from a dog tapeworm. Migration tracks may be seen as dark lines.
  • Hydatid cysts and abscesses.

Kidneys

Kidneys stay in the carcass in small stock. Look for cysts, pale or soft kidneys and discolouration.

Why dog tapeworms matter

Hydatid cysts, sheep measles and bladder worms all come from tapeworms of dogs that eat raw offal on the farm. Recording these findings and giving feedback to farmers helps them deworm farm dogs and stop feeding them raw offal. This is important because hydatid disease can also infect people.

Green offal

View the stomachs and intestines for inflammation and damage, and the mesenteric lymph nodes for abscesses. Spilled gut content must be trimmed off the carcass.

lessons.title: Carcass inspection and judgement of small stock
lessons.html:
Inspecting the carcass

Small stock carcasses are usually not split, so inspect the outside and then the inside through the opened chest and belly.

  • Outer surface: bruises (often from wool pulling), wool and dirt, grass seeds that have pierced the skin, injection lesions.
  • Lymph nodes: palpate the prescapular (in front of the shoulder) and prefemoral (in the flank) lymph nodes. Hard, swollen nodes with green-yellow pus that has an onion-ring look point to caseous lymphadenitis.
  • Inner surfaces: pleurisy, peritonitis, abscesses.
  • Muscle: look at visible cut muscle and the diaphragm for sheep measles cysts.
  • Colour and smell: yellow fat and tissues may mean jaundice; a poorly bled carcass may mean fever.

Judgement examples

FindingUsual action
Single caseous lymphadenitis abscessRemove the node and surrounding area; pass the rest
Many abscesses with poor conditionDetain; may be totally condemned
Bladder worm on omentum or liverRemove affected parts
Sheep measles cystsDetain for the veterinarian; judgement depends on the degree of infestation
Grass seeds in skin and muscleTrim affected areas
Jaundice or generalised diseaseDetain; usually total condemnation

Hygiene and records

Cutting into an abscess spreads pus. If your knife cuts an abscess, stop, trim the contaminated area, and sterilise the knife and wash your hands before the next carcass. Record each condemnation with the producer's name so that farm feedback reports are accurate.

Key points

  • Never lift sheep by the wool; it causes bruising and is inhumane.
  • Hydatid cysts, sheep measles and bladder worms come from dog tapeworms; give farmers feedback.
  • Palpate prescapular and prefemoral lymph nodes for caseous lymphadenitis.
  • Incise the heart for sheep measles and check the liver for fluke and bladder worms.
  • Sterilise the knife after cutting into any abscess.
